messages.body_plain:
Never mind, the irc #R guys helped me out:

attach(contigs)

stat.n50 = aggregate(Contig.Length,list(k=k,name=Organism.Name),n50)
stat.sum = aggregate(Contig.Length,list(k=k,name=Organism.Name),sum)
all = merge(stat.n50,stat.sum,by=c("k","name"))
names(all) = c("Kmer Length","Organism Name","n50","Assembly Length")
summary(all)

Hope this is able to help somebody else.
-r

If I run, e.g.

ggplot(data = diamonds, aes(carat, price)) + geom_hex()

Not the colors that it uses, but where it uses them.  It looks like there is only one hexagon at the highest level (over 7000 or so) and a huge number at
the lowest level.

Can this be adjusted?

Peter

PS I took the "looking at data" course last week - it was excellent!  I am now playing some more with some of the examples Hadley used.

messages.subject: Deducer 0.1 a new R GUI using ggplot2
messages.subject_clean: Deducer 0.1 a new R GUI using ggplot2
messages.body_plain:
Hi everyone,

I just thought I'd let everyone know that I've just released a new
package that makes fairly heavy use of ggplot2. Deducer is a graphical
user interface for data analysis using R. One thing I've tried hard to
do is have every analysis be accompanied by a visualization.

 *one sample tests have histograms
 *t-tests and anovas have box/jitter plots
 *correlations have scatter and cirle plots as well as the excellent
ggcorplot function (discussed on this list) written by Mike Lawrence
 *Regressions have diagnostic and effect plots
 *Logistic regression also has ROC plots

Most of these visualizations are made using ggplot2. In the future
Deducer will have a separate 'Plot' menu for creating standard plots.
I welcome feedback from the community (either on list or privately).
You can check out the manual at:

http://www.deducer.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php?n=Main.DeducerManual

And I've created a new mailing list which you can follow if
interested.

http://groups.google.com/group/deducer

Let me know what you think,
Ian

p.s. Installation instructions:
install.packages("Deducer",,"http://cran.r-project.org")

---------------------------------------------------------------------------

Deducer 0.1 has been released to CRAN

Deducer is designed to be a free, easy to use, alternative to
proprietary
software such as SPSS, JMP, and Minitab. It has a menu system to do
common
data manipulation and data analysis tasks, and an excel-like
spreadsheet in
which to view and edit data frames. The goal of the project is to two
fold.

        1. Provide an intuitive interface so that non-technical users
           can learn and perform analyses without programming getting
           in their way.
        2. Increase the efficiency of expert R users when performing
         common tasks by replacing hundreds of keystrokes with a few
         mouse clicks. Also, as much as possible the GUI should not
         get in their way if they just want to do some programming.

Deducer is integrated into the Windows RGui, and the cross-platform
Java
console JGR, and is also usable and accessible from the command line.
Screen shots and examples can be viewed in the online wiki manual:

http://www.deducer.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php?n=Main.DeducerManual

Comments and questions are more than welcome. A discussion group has
been
created for any questions or recommendations.

http://groups.google.com/group/deducer

Deducer Features:

Data manipulation:
        1. Factor editor
        2. Variable recoding
        3. data sorting
        4. data frame merging
        5. transposing a data frame
        6. subseting

Analysis:
        1. Frequencies
        2. Descriptives
        3. Contingency tables
                a. Nicely formatted tables with optional
                        i. Percentages
                        ii. Expected counts
                        iii. Residuals
                b. Statistical tests
                        i. chi-squared
                        ii. likelihood ratio
                        iii. fisher's exact
                        iv. mantel haenszel
                        v. kendall's tau
                        vi. spearman's rho
                        vii. kruskal-wallis
                        viii. mid-p values for all exact/monte carlo
tests
        4. One sample tests
                a. T-test
                b. Shapiro-wilk
                c. Histogram/box-plot summaries
        5. Two sample tests
                a. T-test (student and welch)
                b. Permutation test
                c. Wilcoxon
                d. Brunner-munzel
                e. Kolmogorov-smirnov
                f. Jitter/box-plot group comparison
        6. K-sample tests
                a. Anova (usual and welch)
                b. Kruskal-wallis
                c. Jitter/boxplot comparison
        7. Correlation
                a. Nicely formatted correlation matrices
                b. Pearson's
                c. Kendall's
                d. Spearman's
                e. Scatterplot paneled array
                f. Circle plot
                g. Full correlation matrix plot
        8.Generalized Linear Models
                a. Model preview
                b. Intuitive model builder
                c. diagnostic plots
                d. Component residual and added variable plots
                e. Anova (type II and III implementing LR, Wald and F
tests)
                f. Parameter summary tables and parameter correlations
                g. Influence and colinearity diagnostics
                h. Post-hoc tests and confidence intervals
                   with (or without) adjustments for multiple testing.
                i. Custom linear hypothesis tests
                j. Effect mean summaries (with confidence intervals),
                   and plots
                k. Exports: Residuals, Standardized residuals,
Studentized
                    residuals, Predicted Values (linear and link),
Cooks
                   distance, DFBETA, DFFITS, hat values, and Cov Ratio
                l. Observation weights and subseting
        9. Logistic Regression
                a. All GLM features
                b. ROC Plot
        10. Linear Model
                a. All GLM features
         b. Heteroskedastic robust tests

messages.subject: Instead of double y-axis
messages.body_plain:
Hello,

As it appears that there is no way to plot 2 y-axis in ggplot, I would
be interested in your viewpoint about the best way to plot these data:

I am surveying mortality during experiments where I change gradually a
parameter (the temperature).
Before using ggplot2 (really great any way ;) I was plotting the
number of individuals against time, and added a second y-axis to plot
temperature against time.

I thought about (i) adding text labels, which is not really satisfying
since I would like to be able to read precisely temperature between
two labels; (ii) adding a color rectangle with a gradient in the
background, but it is not so straight forward and does not give access
to precise temperature data; (iii) superimposing two plots one for the
temperature, the other for the number of individuals.

Is there a another (better) option? concerning the faceting with
different axis, what is the best option? is there a lighter way than
viewports?

Thank you in advance,

Thomas

pl.test <- ggplot( ) +
  layer(data=test.df.vline, mapping=aes(color = col, x=ext.mean, y=zer, xend = ext.mean,), geom="vline", stat="identity", position="identity") +
  layer( data=test.df, mapping =aes (x=xv, y=yv, color=lv), geom="line")
pl.test

Keith

Well sorry if I wasted your time with this issue.  I'm getting close to what I was hoping for.  I'll post the sample chart and the code that made it, in case it might help someone else.

The chart has a geom_line, and geom_vline, and a geom_rect (all using different data frames.)   I'm not sure about the xend parameter for the vline layer.  May not be necessary, but I saw an error when it was absent that led me to add it.

#make a simple pyradmid shape
yv <- c( seq(1,100), seq( 101,1))
xv <-  seq(-1200,-1000)
lv <- c("series1")
test.df <- as.data.frame( yv )
test.df$xv <- xv
test.df$lv <- lv

#put a value for the vline in a df
ext.mean <- c( -1105.4)
test.df.vline <- as.data.frame( ext.mean  )
test.df.vline$col <- c("other mean")
test.df.vline$zer <- c(0)

#make a data frame for a rectangle
xmin <- c( -1111.4)
test.df.rect <- as.data.frame( xmin  )
test.df.rect$xmax <- c( -1058.2)
test.df.rect$ymin <- c( 0)
test.df.rect$ymax <- c( 100)
test.df.rect$col <- c( "other s.d.")

pl.test <- ggplot( )+
     scale_fill_manual (name="Fill",  values=c( alpha("tan", 0.2))  ) + scale_colour_brewer (name="Legend"  ) +
  layer( data=test.df, mapping =aes (x=xv, y=yv, color=lv), geom="line") +
  layer( data=test.df.rect, mapping=aes(xmin = xmin, xmax = xmax, ymin=ymin, ymax=ymax,  fill=col  ), geom="rect")  +

  layer(data=test.df.vline, mapping=aes(color = col, x=ext.mean, y=zer, xend = ext.mean,), geom="vline", stat="identity", position="identity")

pl.test <- pl.test +  scale_x_continuous (  breaks =c(-1100) , limits=c(-1150, -1050))

pl.test

messages.subject: Re: Instead of double y-axis
messages.body_plain:
My understanding of Hadley's opinion regarding two y-axes and his
intention with ggplot2, based on a read of his book, is to
purposefully omit double y-axes in favor of using one of two options:
1) rebase your series so that they fit onto a common y-axis, or 2) use
facet_grid to create two charts (one above the other, for example) to
show comparative movement on independent y-axes. If you use the second
option, consider setting scale="free-y" or even scale="free" as
appropriate.

I hope this helps you.

Michael

messages.subject: Re: order results ignored
messages.body_plain:
For a given factor, say df$name, you can reorder for example like this:

df$name <- factor(df$name,
   levels=c("Max out degree","Max impact",
            "Min out degree","Min impact")
)

After that, ggplot2 uses the new order of df$name ...

With ezLev its almost the same length of code. So I do not see the
nessecity for using an extra package like ez:

df$name <- ezLev(
   x=df$name,
   new_order=c("Max out degree","Max impact",
               "Min out degree","Min impact")
)

Rainer Hurling

People more expert than I can help with the ggplot code, but I am wondering what you really want here.

If you do two histograms on top of each other, then it is going to be hard to read.  Things will overlap.  Also, the
scales for the log and the untransformed variable with be very different, this will make the choice of bin width problematic,
as it is likely that the log variable should have a smaller bin width.

Perhaps you want two density curves?

Are you perhaps doing this to demonstrate how logs work?

messages.subject: Combining plots and tables on single PDF page
messages.subject_clean: Combining plots and tables on single PDF page
messages.body_plain:
All:

For the last few days I have been trying to create a single page in
PDF with 8 viewports.  Four of the viewports are to hold graphics
developed using ggplot2.  The other four are to hold simple printouts
of data frames.  Creating and placing the four graphs has been real
easy!  Getting the data frames to print in the correct viewports has
been a nightmare.  The best I can do is to have all the tables print
in the middle of the page, over the graphs and over each other.   At
this point, I do not want to learn Latex, Weave (in its various
flavors) and the like.  I still need to master R more before I feel
comfortable adding additional layers of complexity.  Also,
restrictions on my computer do not allow me to install all Latex
completely.  Anyway,  here are the key excerpts from the code. If
anyone has any ideas, I would be very appreciative.

Thanks!

Gene

#####  Helper function to push individual viewports
##### Source: Hadley, ggplot2, p. 154)

vplayout <- function(x, y)
  {
     viewport(layout.pos.row = x, layout.pos.col = y)
  }

##### Generate Report Page

create_page <- function(rate_ticker)
  {

    # Assign function outputs to variables

    p1 <- full_plot(rate_ticker)                  # graph
    p2 <- daily_diff_plot(rate_ticker)         # graph
    p3 <- daily_hist_plot(rate_ticker)        # graph
    p4 <- daily_scatter_plot(rate_ticker)   # graph
    p5 <- table_1(rate_ticker)                  # dataframe
    p6 <- table_2(rate_ticker)                  # dataframe
    p7 <- table_3(rate_ticker)                  # dataframe

    # Structure the page

    plot.new <http://plot.new>()
    pushViewport(viewport(layout = grid.layout(4,2)))

    # place graphs in their inidividual viewports  - NOTE: This works
fine
    print(p1, vp = vplayout(1,1), newpage = FALSE)
    print(p2, vp = vplayout(1,2), newpage = FALSE)
    print(p3, vp = vplayout(2,1), newpage = FALSE)
    print(p4, vp = vplayout(2,2), newpage = FALSE)

    # place tables in their inidividual viewports  - NOTE: The tables
print oput, but they overwrite the
    # graphs and each other.
    pushViewport(viewport(layout = grid.layout(3,1)))
    par(new = TRUE)
    textplot(p5, halign = "center", valign = "center", show.rownames =
FALSE)

    pushViewport(viewport(layout = grid.layout(3,2)))
    par(new = TRUE)
    textplot(p6[1:15,], halign = "center", valign = "center",
show.rownames = FALSE)

    pushViewport(viewport(layout = grid.layout(4,1)))
    par(new = TRUE)
    textplot(p7[1:15,], halign = "center", valign = "center",
show.rownames = FALSE)
   }

##### Call function (pass ticker) to generate page

pdf.options(height = 11, width  = 8.5, paper  = "letter")
pdf("./Output/June2009.pdf")
create_page("US0003M")
dev.off()

messages.subject: Re: Adding a geom_vline layer
messages.body_plain:
Hi Keith,

You should be using xintercept with geom_vline:

ggplot() +
  geom_line(aes(x = xv, y = yv, color = lv), test.df) +
  geom_rect(aes(xmin = xmin, xmax = xmax, ymin = ymin, ymax = ymax, fill=col),
    test.df.rect)  +
  geom_vline(aes(color = col, xintercept=ext.mean), test.df.vline) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = -1100, limits = c(-1150, -1050)) +
  scale_fill_manual(name="Fill", values = alpha("tan", 0.2)) +
  scale_colour_brewer(name="Legend")

I really recommend using the geom functions rather than the more
general layer function because you can more easily scan the start of
each line to see what it's doing.

Hadley

messages.body_plain:
Hi Szilard -

Try this with the d variable you provided :

  df  <- d
  n   <- 201
  rng <- extendrange(df$value)
  x   <- seq(rng[1], rng[2], length = n)

  ecdf_wrapper <- function(df){
   data.frame(
     gr = df$gr[1],
     variable = df$variable[1],
     x = x,
     Fx = ecdf(df$value)(x)
   )
  }
  df <- ddply(df, .(gr, variable), ecdf_wrapper)

  qplot(x, Fx, data = df, geom = 'step', colour = gr, facets = . ~ variable)

Is that what you're looking for?

Let me know how it goes
david.

messages.subject: Re: Cum % Stacked Bar
messages.body_plain:
Try the following

df$glaucoma <- factor(df$glaucoma)

# This is the quick way of getting a bar chart, but it is not possible
to plot text labels this way
ggplot(data.frame(table(df)), aes(age, Freq, label = Freq, fill =
glaucoma)) +
	geom_bar(position = "fill") +
	scale_y_continuous(formatter = "percent") +
	scale_fill_hue(labels = c("No Glaucoma", "Glaucoma"))

# To plot text labels as well, you would need to calculate the
percentages, and text label positions # manually
x <- ddply(df, .(age, glaucoma), summarise, fr = length
(glaucoma), .drop = F)
x <- ddply(x, .(age), transform, fr_pc = fr/sum(fr))
x <- ddply(x, .(age), transform, txt_pos = cumsum(fr_pc) - fr_pc/2)

ggplot(x, aes(age, fr_pc, label = fr, fill = rev(glaucoma))) +
	geom_bar(stat = "identity") +
	geom_text(aes(y = txt_pos)) +
	scale_y_continuous("", formatter = "percent") 	+
 	scale_fill_hue("",labels = c("Glaucoma", "No Glaucoma"))

--

messages.body_plain:
Here is a working example.   I can get the four plots to display
nicely in the
first four viewports I created on the PDF device...but the four tables
I am trying to place on the other four viewports on the same page
using
textplot to first conver them into plots, but they end up on separate
pages.

Any suggestions on this or any other method for getting graphs and
tables to display
on the same page?  Again, I would like to stay away from Sweave and
Latex technologies
for now.

Thanks!

Gene

require(ggplot2)
require(gplots)
require(grDevices)
set.seed(1410)
dsmall <- diamonds[sample(nrow(diamonds), 100), ]
dtable <- dsmall[1:10, 1:5]

a <- qplot(carat, price, data = dsmall, colour = color)
b <- qplot(log(carat), log(price), data = dsmall)
c <- qplot(carat, x * y * z, data = dsmall)
d <- qplot(carat, price, data = dsmall, alpha = I(1/10))

pdf("./Output/test.pdf", width = 8, height = 11.5)
grid.newpage()

pushViewport(viewport(layout = grid.layout(4,2)))

print(a, vp = viewport(layout.pos.row = 1, layout.pos.col = 1))
print(b, vp = viewport(layout.pos.row = 1, layout.pos.col = 2))
print(c, vp = viewport(layout.pos.row = 2, layout.pos.col = 1))
print(d, vp = viewport(layout.pos.row = 2, layout.pos.col = 2))
pushViewport(viewport(layout.pos.row = 3, layout.pos.col = 1))
textplot(dtable)
pushViewport(viewport(layout.pos.row = 3, layout.pos.col = 2))
textplot(dtable)
pushViewport(viewport(layout.pos.row = 4, layout.pos.col = 1))
textplot(dtable)
pushViewport(viewport(layout.pos.row = 4, layout.pos.col = 2))
textplot(dtable)

dev.off()

messages.body_plain:
Thanks LearnR for very efficient/compact solution.

However, some of my variables have a considerable part of their
distribution at the lowest value (at 0), and it would be nice therefore
for the ECDF line to start at (0,0) (actually (xmin,0) more generally).
I came up with inserting this code before the plot:
dp <- ddply(dp, .(gr, variable), function(df) {

  rbind(data.frame(gr=df$gr[1],
                   variable=df$variable[1],
                   value=min(df$value),

                   ecdf=0), df)
})
but I wonder if there is a better way to do that.

Szilard

messages.body_plain:
Hi,

you could perhaps try the gridBase package, designed to mix Grid and
Base graphics. Here is a small example,

require(ggplot2)
require(gridBase)

require(gplots)
require(grDevices)
set.seed(1410)
dsmall <- diamonds[sample(nrow(diamonds), 100), ]
dtable <- dsmall[1:10, 1:5]

a <- qplot(carat, price, data = dsmall, colour = color)

pdf("test.pdf", width = 10, height = 10)
plot.new <http://plot.new>()
pushViewport(viewport(layout = grid.layout(2,1)))

print(a, vp = viewport(layout.pos.row = 1, layout.pos.col = 1))

pushViewport(viewport(layout.pos.row = 2, layout.pos.col = 1))
par(plt=gridPLT(), new=TRUE,ps=8)
textplot(dtable,valign="bottom")
dev.off()

The alignment of textplot() on a page seems trickier than a simple
plot(), though. It may be worthwhile writing a similar code in pure
Grid (I once saw some tutorials on tables on Paul Murrell's webpage).

HTH,

baptiste

Baptiste

Thanks for the suggestion.  Hadley had mentioned something along those
same lines.  The issue does appear to be - as you suggest - one of
lining up the grid graph device and the base graph device. If you
remove the valign from your code you can see that the table is really
centered on the whole graph device, rather than the viewport.  I
suspect the issue lies with the use of the gridPLT() function as I am
not properly converting location between the two grids.    I will look
up Murrell's work to see if he has dealt with this issue.  Thanks
again for the thoughts.. they have really helped to clarify my
thinking.

Cheers,

Gene

messages.body_plain:
If you're willing to play with Grid, I found the document I mentioned earlier,

www.stat.auckland.ac.nz/~paul/grid/doc/R-1.8.0/table.pdf <http://www.stat.auckland.ac.nz/~paul/grid/doc/R-1.8.0/table.pdf>

It seems a little outdated though. I managed to get two basic tables
to work that you might find useful as a starting point,

labels <- c("n", "average", "std.dev <http://std.dev>")
values <- c(7, 15.833, 9.58)

# with a manual layout, probably not the best route...

the.layout <- grid.layout(3, 2, widths = unit(c(1, 1), "inches"),
 heights = unit(rep(1, 3), "lines"))
 pushViewport(viewport(layout = the.layout))
 for (row in 1:3) {
 pushViewport(viewport(layout.pos.col = 1, layout.pos.row = row))
 grid.rect()
 grid.text(labels[row], x = unit(0.1, "inches"), just = c("left",
 "centre"))
popViewport()
 pushViewport(viewport(layout.pos.col = 2, layout.pos.row = row))
 grid.rect()

 grid.text(values[row], x = unit(1, "npc") - unit(0.1, "inches"),
 just = c("right", "centre"))
popViewport()
 }
 popViewport()

# using frames, much easier to wrap in a function

grid.frame(name="gf",
	layout = grid.layout(3, 2, width = unit(c(1, 1), "inches"),
								heights = unit(rep(1, 3), "lines")),
	draw = TRUE)

for (col in 1:2) {
 for (row in 1:3) {
  grid.place("gf", rectGrob(gp=gpar(fill="grey")), row=row,col=col)
  grid.place("gf", textGrob(paste("label",row, ",",col)) , row=row,col=col)
 }
}

A more recent document ("Drawing Diagrams with R") provides an example
of automated string width calculation. It would be nice to wrap
something like this into a generic function with a method for
data.frames.

Best wishes,

baptiste

messages.subject: Re: trouble with grouped box plots
messages.body_plain:
Maybe it's just easier to do it all by hand, and drop geom_boxplot altogether:

b <- read.table("http://mickmcquaid.com/unevensample",header=T)
out <- ddply(b, c("j", "k"), summarise, out = boxplot.stats(i,coef=1.4)$out)

stats <- ddply(b, c("j", "k"), function(df) boxplot.stats(df$i,coef=1.4)$stats)
names(stats)[-(1:2)] <- c("lwhisker", "lhinge", "med", "uhinge", "uwhisker")

ggplot(stats, aes(k, med, fill = k, colour = k)) +
  geom_segment(aes(xend = k, y = lwhisker, yend = uwhisker)) +
  geom_crossbar(aes(ymin = lhinge, ymax = uhinge)) +
  geom_crossbar(aes(ymin = med, ymax = med), color = "grey90") +
  geom_point(aes(y = out), out) +
  facet_grid(. ~ j)

What do you think?

Hadley

passed internally to kde2d. This affects the amount of smoothing and
is not the same as the default. Because of the way the code is
written, the user cannot pass a different value to override n=100.

I wonder if there is a workaround to this limitation and whether or
not it might be changed in a subsequent release.

d = data.frame(x=2:7)
dd = transform(d, ecdf=ecdf(x)(x))

qplot(x, ecdf, data=dd, geom='step') + ylim(c(0,1))

and this:

dd2 = rbind( data.frame(x=min(d$x), ecdf=0), dd )
qplot(x, ecdf, data=dd2, geom='step') + ylim(c(0,1))

I would prefer the 2nd, where the steps start from y=0.

>From this point of view the previous solution given by David fits better:

resolution = 1000
rng = extendrange(d$x)
xsteps = seq(rng[1], rng[2], length = resolution)
dd3 = data.frame( x = xsteps, ecdf = ecdf(d$x)(xsteps) )

qplot(x, ecdf, data=dd3, geom='step') + ylim(c(0,1))

However, in this case setting resolution very low would distort the
plot, while having it very high might slow down the plot in case of many
variables (groups/facets).

messages.subject: grob names into grobs?
messages.body_plain:
Hello ggplot2'ers,

I have a number of graphic objects (grobs) that I created with ggplot2 and have prefixed their names with "g_".

e.g. g_x_and_y_by_zcat
> class( g_x_and_y_by_zcat )
[1] "ggplot"

> graphs         <- grep("^g_", ls(), value=TRUE )
> class(graphs)
[1] "character"

Essentially, I am trying to write a function that will parse out elements in the name of a grob,  create a relevant PNG filename, and then print the grob to the pngfile.  The goal is that I'd also like this to operate on all the graphs in my "graphs" object which contains all my grob names, hopefully using the Plyr library ( perhaps l_ply I think...), such that the output will be PNG files containing the graphs

I imagine the function will be something like:

draw_graph <- function( grobname ) {
	png_fn = paste( grobname, ".png", sep="")
	print( png_fn )
	png( filename=png_fn )
	  print( grobname )
	dev.off()
}

...followed by the use of l_ply.

This doesn't quite work however, because the print(grobname) is evaluating as a name rather than as the gglot2 object that I would like it to be.  I have been playing with do.call() with as.list(graphs) to try to coerce this to evaluate, but so far without success.

Is there a way to do this?

Any help appreciated.

Thanks,
Avram

messages.subject: Changing legend labels with scale_colour_gradientn
messages.body_plain:
I am having difficulties in changing the labels of a legend generated
by scale_colour_gradientn - it seems that the labels argument has no
effect on the outcome.

Consider the following example:
dsub <- subset(diamonds, x > 5 & x < 6 & y > 5 & y < 6)
dsub$diff <- with(dsub, sqrt(abs(x-y))* sign(x-y))
d <- qplot(x, y, data=dsub, colour=diff)

nbr <- 5
breaks <- seq(-0.4, 0.6, length.out = nbr)
nlabel = letters[1:nbr]
d + scale_colour_gradientn(colour = rainbow(7), breaks = breaks, label
= nlabel)

The breaks have been updated, but not the labels.

Any ideas how to get around this?

--
http://learnr.wordpress.com

messages.body_plain:
As noted earlier on this list, best practice is to include an example
data set. Here's a hacky way of creating one, then code to create the
graph you illustrated:

seed = 1
temp = expand.grid(
	A = c('A1','A2')
	, B = c('B1','B2')
	, C = c('C1','C2')
)
temp$temp = sample(1:8)

my_data = NULL
for(i in 1:length(temp$temp)){
	for(j in 1:temp$temp[i]){
		my_data = rbind(my_data,temp[i,1:3])
	}
}

ggplot(
	data = my_data
	, mapping = aes(
		x = A
		, fill = B
	)
)+
geom_bar()+facet_grid(.~C)

messages.subject: Problem with geom_text
messages.body_plain:
Hi

I have a problem with geom_text. For example following code works:

qplot(x = cyl, y = disp,  data = mtcars) + geom_text(data =
data.frame( x = 6, y= 10), map=aes(x=x, y=y), label = "Text")

However, adding a colour variable breaks the code. For example:

> qplot(x = cyl, y = disp,  data = mtcars, colour = cyl) + geom_text(data = data.frame( x = 6, y= 10), map=aes(x=x, y=y), label = "Text")
Error in eval(expr, envir, enclos) : object 'cyl' not found

It seems that it does not want to create new layer for text, even
though I have explicitly created new data frame for it. Is there some
way I can avoid the problem?

Best,
Raivo

messages.subject: Re: Problem with geom_text
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I believe the problem is that the new layer inherits the aesthetic
mapping for colour defined in the qplot() call, i.e. it looks for a
variable cyl in the data.frame supplied to geom_text and fails to find
one. You can specifically tell geom_text not to bother with this
mapping, or use annotate,

qplot(x = cyl, y = disp,  data = mtcars, colour = cyl) +
geom_text(data = data.frame( x = 6, y= 10), map=aes(x=x, y=y),

colour="black", label = "Text")

qplot(x = cyl, y = disp,  data = mtcars, colour = cyl) +

annotate(geom="text", x = 6, y= 10, colour="black", label = "Text" )

HTH,

baptiste

messages.subject: Re: Increasing size of labels
messages.body_plain:
Hi Tony, just add the following

#to save some of the rewriting
size20 <- theme_text(size=20)

l1+l2+l3+l4+scale_colour_manual("Year", c("2004"="orange", "2007"="green")) +
  opts(axis.text.y = size20, axis.text.x = size20, axis.title.y = size20, axis.title.x = size20,
  legend.text = size20)

That's an example, you could change the size with any value that works for you. Also, you could write:

opts(axis.title.x = theme_text( size = 30))

again change the size for the one that works for you.
If you are using that size a lot you could save to a theme so you save a lot of time
I don't know if there's any easier solution to this.

I hope it helps.

messages.subject: Ljung-Box statistic code with ggplot
messages.body_plain:
I apply to solve time series analysis but I have problem
related to  Ljung-Box statistic code.(above)

Can you help me to solve Ljung-Box statistic code problem for
in this example ?

######################## ACF ########### PACF ###########

d  <- acf(v, plot=FALSE)
df <- data.frame(d$lag, d$acf)
p  <- ggplot(df, aes(d.lag, d.acf))
p + geom_bar(stat='identity', aes(width=0.2))+ geom_hline
(yintercept=1)
ggsave(file="ACF.png",width=8,height=6)

dp  <- pacf(v, plot=FALSE)
df <- data.frame(dp$lag, dp$acf)
p  <- ggplot(df, aes(dp.lag, dp.acf))
p + geom_bar(stat='identity', aes(width=0.1))
ggsave(file="PACF.png",width=8,height=6)

######################## Model Building#######################

fitmodel<- arima(v,order=c(4,1,0))
fitmodel
tsdiag(fitmodel)

# Standardized residual

stdres <- as.numeric(resid(fitmodel) / sqrt(fitmodel$sigma2))
qplot(seq_along(stdres), stdres, yend = 0, xend = seq_along(stdres),
geom="segment") + geom_hline(colour = "grey50")
ggsave(file="S.residual.png",width=8,height=6)

# ACF

acf <- acf(resid(fitmodel), plot = F)
acf_df <- data.frame(acf = acf$acf,lag = acf$lag)

conint <- 0.95
conlim <- qnorm((1 + conint)/2) / sqrt(acf$n.used)

qplot(lag, acf, data = acf_df, yend = 0, xend = lag, geom="segment") +
geom_hline(colour = "grey") +
geom_point() +
geom_hline(yintercept = c(-conlim, conlim), colour = "red")
ggsave(file="ACF.RES.png",width=8,height=6)

###################  Ljung-Box statistic #######################

ljungbox <- function(i, rs) { Box.test(rs, i, type = "Ljung-Box")
$p.value }

acf_df$pvalue <- sapply(acf_df$lag, ljungbox, series = resid(fit))

qplot(lag, pvalue, data = acf_df) + geom_hline(colour = "grey50") +
geom_hline(yintercept = 0.05, colour = "darkblue")

messages.subject: Clip data to zoom color scales (suggestion with workaround)
messages.subject_clean: Clip data to zoom color scales (suggestion with workaround)
messages.body_plain:
I would like to set manual limits on the colour scale when using
geom_tile, so that outliers will not compress the color scale for the
remaining values. Although I can specify a limits= argument to
scale_fill_continuous and friends, values outside the limits leave
gaps in the plot.

What I'm after is similar functionality for the color axis as for x
and y axes, which have separate limits on scales and coordinate
systems (cf. chapter 7.3.3 of the ggplot2 book). Scale limits subset
the data, whereas coordinate limits just perform a visual zoom.

I'm working around this problem as shown below, using a stat to clip
values to specified limits. Here's a shortened version of the example,
assuming stat_clip is defined as below.

library(reshape)
x <- melt(matrix(c(-10,1:10,20),3,4)) # sample data with outliers
clim <- c(3,8) # color axis limits
p <- qplot(X1, X2, data=x, geom="tile", fill=value) +
scale_fill_continuous(limits=clim)
p + geom_text(aes(label=value))   # plot with gaps
p + stat_clip(limits=clim) + geom_text(aes(label=value))   # plot
without gaps

I'm posting it here in case it might be useful to others; if there are
neater ways to do this (e.g. getting the limits from the argument
passed to the colour scale), I'd be happy to learn.

Best regards,
Jon Olav

== stat_clip.R ==
# stat_clip to zoom color scales without hiding data that fall outside
limits
library(ggplot2)

clip <- function(x, limits=c(-Inf, Inf))
    pmin(pmax(limits[1], x), limits[2])

StatClip <- proto(Stat, {
    objname <- "clip"
    desc <- "Replace extreme data by lower and upper limits"

    # # Unfortunately, setting default_geom here will override the
geom_text()
    # # used in the example below.
    default_geom <- function(.) GeomTile
    calculate_groups <- function(., data, limits=c(-Inf, Inf), ...) {
        # print(data) # useful to see what's available for the
function
        data$fill <- clip(data$fill, limits)
        return(data)
        }
    icon <- function(.) textGrob("f(x) = clip(x,xmin,xmax)", gp=gpar
(cex=1.2))

    desc_outputs <- list()

    examples <- function(.) {
        # Zoom color scale without omitting values outside limits
        library(reshape)
        x <- melt(matrix(c(-10,1:10,20),3,4)) # sample data with
outliers
        clim <- c(3,8) # color axis limits
        p <- qplot(X1, X2, data=x, geom="tile", fill=value) +
            geom_text(aes(label=value)) + theme_bw()
        plots <- list(p, p + scale_fill_continuous(limits=clim),
            p + scale_fill_continuous(limits=clim) +
                stat_clip(limits=clim) + geom_text(aes(label=value))
        )
        # adapted from ggplot book chapter 8.4.2, "rectangular grids"
        vp <- function(i) viewport(layout.pos.row=1, layout.pos.col=i)
        grid.newpage()
        pushViewport(viewport(layout=grid.layout(1,3)))
        invisible(mapply(print, plots, vp=lapply(1:3,vp)))
    }
})

stat_clip <- StatClip$build_accessor()

StatClip$examples()

messages.subject: Re: Clip data to zoom color scales (suggestion with workaround)
messages.subject_clean: Clip data to zoom color scales (suggestion with workaround)
messages.body_plain:
On Sat, Aug 22, 2009 at 7:35 AM, Jon Olav Vik<jon...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> I would like to set manual limits on the colour scale when using
> geom_tile, so that outliers will not compress the color scale for the
> remaining values. Although I can specify a limits= argument to
> scale_fill_continuous and friends, values outside the limits leave
> gaps in the plot.
>
> What I'm after is similar functionality for the color axis as for x
> and y axes, which have separate limits on scales and coordinate
> systems (cf. chapter 7.3.3 of the ggplot2 book). Scale limits subset
> the data, whereas coordinate limits just perform a visual zoom.

Hmmm, I disagree that this is equivalent to coordinate zooming, but I
can see how it would be useful.  I'd suggest making it slightly more
general by using the following (untested) calculate_groups function:

calculate_groups <- function(., data, limits = list(), ...) {
  for(aes in names(limits)) {
    data[[aes]] <- clip(data[[aes]], limits[[aes]])
  }
  data
}

Then you could say stat_clip(limits = list(fill = c(1, 5), x = c(1, 5)) etc.

Hadley

--

messages.subject: Re: Linetypes
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

It's easy to use custom linetypes but only in terms of spacing
specification, I believe (as in the rest of R graphics). See this
example,

library(maps)
states = map_data("state")
statenames = unique(states$region)
states <- subset(states, region %in% statenames[sample(1:length(statenames),5)])

ltys = c("22", "44", "13", "1343", "73", "2262", "12223242", "F282",
"F4448444", "224282F2", "F1")

qplot(long, lat, data = states, group = group,
	linetype = factor(region), geom="path") +
	scale_linetype_manual(values = ltys[1:5])

Making double lines and ladder-lines as you call them should be doable
if you superpose different geoms on top of each other, but it's
probably hard to automate. Try this for instance,

qplot(long, lat, data = states, group = group, geom="path",
	linetype=I("solid"), size=I(2)) +
      geom_path(size=1, colour="grey95") # match the background colour

HTH,

baptiste

you must use viewports with ggplot2 in order to obtain multiple graphics in a single figure. As far as I know par options doesn't affect graphics made with ggplot2.
Here is an example code to do what you want. I hope it helps.
Bye

p1 = ggplot(...)+...
p2 = ggplot(...)+...
p3 = ggplot(...)+...
p4 = ggplot(...)+...

vplayout <- function(x, y) viewport(layout.pos.row=x, layout.pos.col=y)
grid.newpage()
pushViewport(viewport(layout=grid.layout(2,2)))

print(p1, vp=vplayout(1,1))
print(p2, vp=vplayout(1,2))
print(p3, vp=vplayout(2,1))
print(p4, vp=vplayout(2,2))

messages.subject: Scales and space in faceting
messages.body_plain:
According to the documentation in Chapter 7,
"For facet_grid there is an additional parameter called space, which
takes
values "free" or "fixed". When the space can vary freely, each column
(or
row) will have width (or height) proportional to the range of the
scale for that
column (or row)."

I'm getting unpredictable behavior when using scales="free_y",
space="free". Take the following example:

da <- data.frame(
     x=rep(1:5, 2),
     y=c(1+(0:4), 1+(0:4)/10),
     z=rep(1:2, each=5))
da

#   x   y z
#1  1 1.0 1
#2  2 2.0 1
#3  3 3.0 1
#4  4 4.0 1
#5  5 5.0 1
#6  1 1.0 2
#7  2 1.1 2
#8  3 1.2 2
#9  4 1.3 2
#10 5 1.4 2

qplot(x, y, data=da, group=z, geom="line") +
#    scale_y_log10() +
     facet_grid(z~., scales="free_y", space="free")

If the facet heights were proportional to their row ranges, the ratio
of the top to bottom facet heights (i.e., z=1 to z=2), should be (5-1)/
(1.4-1) = 4/0.4 = 10. The observed ratio in the resulting plot is
actually a lot smaller than that.

If you uncomment the log10 option, this problem looks worse: the two
heights now look the same! Instead, the heights ratio should be
log10(5)/log10(1.4) (since log10(1) = 0), i.e., 4.78.

Comments? I'm using R 2.9.1 and ggplot2 0.8.3.

Roberto
